title: Duct System Pressure Explorer
description: Five calculation challenges on an illustrative exhaust system (inlet velocity, outlet velocity pressure, fan total pressure, air power, and pressure at 20% more airflow), each with its target readout hidden until checked, followed by free exploration of the airflow with live station and fan values.
creator: Twin City Fan
subject: airflow continuity equation
velocity pressure
total pressure
fan total pressure
fan static pressure
air power
system resistance relation

educational.audience: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff
educational.topic: Velocity pressure, total pressure, fan pressure rise and air power in a duct system
learningObjectives: The learner will calculate duct velocity, velocity pressure, total pressure, fan total pressure and air power for a simple exhaust duct system, to within the tolerances stated in Feedback.

accessibility.notes: describe() text (fallback mode); verdicts, each new challenge, definitions and the end summary announced through FP.announce (aria-live); ✓/✗ glyphs and solid/dashed borders pair with colour; hidden readouts show '?'; Enter checks and goes to the next challenge; schematic definitions also reachable from the 'Definition of…' select; the answer box, buttons, select and slider are reachable with Tab.

equations: FTP = TP2 - TP1; FSP = FTP - VP2
rules: Velocities shown to 10 fpm, pressures to 0.01 in. wg, air power to 0.01 hp, from unrounded intermediates
Challenge tolerances: ±25 fpm, ±0.02, ±0.03, ±0.05 hp, ±0.05 in. wg around the spec answers 2,500, 0.81, 3.62, 5.70, 5.21
Two attempts per challenge; the target readout is hidden until the challenge resolves
assumptions: Illustrative system whose total pressures follow the system resistance relation from the 10,000 CFM worked example
limitations: No fixed (non-square-law) pressure component in the system
Velocity is the average across each duct section

sources: Chapter 2 sections 'Velocity Pressure', 'Pressure Rise and Air Power' and 'The Duct System' (worked examples at 10,000 and 12,000 CFM)

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Practice with check: the target readout stays hidden until the learner commits a number, then guided exploration of the airflow
keyQuestions: Why does subtracting a negative inlet total pressure add to the fan's pressure rise?
Why does a 30% smaller duct roughly double the velocity pressure?
Why does 20% more airflow need 44% more pressure and 73% more air power?
commonMisconceptions: Inlet static pressure is added as a positive number
Velocity pressure is proportional to velocity rather than velocity squared
A 20 percent airflow increase needs only 20 percent more pressure
Static pressure always falls in the direction of flow
assessmentOpportunities: First-attempt score shown as 'Challenges correct: n of 5'; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt.
